doc_summary: HCAST is a 189-task autonomy benchmark grounded in human-baseline completion times, built with heavy manual QA and transcript review. The paper is explicit about where its tasks are realistic and where they are not.

items.claim: prefers tasks derived from real-world work and open-ended, multi-step environments over narrow or toy question-style benchmarks because scores on the latter are not predictive of real-world competence.
items.quote: Many existing benchmarks measure AI performance on challenging questions or problems that require significant domain expertise (Rein et al., 2023; Glazer et al., 2024). These capture models’ extensive expert-level knowledge and domain-specific reasoning skills. However, they are not necessarily predictive of real-world competence and usefulness.

items.claim: In a setup, use novel, privately authored problems that require real adaptation instead of publicly available or easily memorized ones because memorization and contamination undermine realism and validity.
items.quote: Require novel solutions to open-ended problems, to avoid concerns about memorization and data contamination, and to increase the realism of evaluations.

items.claim: In a setup, source scenarios from independent contributors who submit tasks from their own work instead of relying only on in-house designers because independence yields more diverse and realistic tasks.
items.quote: The bounty program solicited task ideas and implementations from independent contributors, whose independence enabled them to submit more diverse and realistic tasks.

items.claim: Reads every agent transcript, successes and failures alike, to check that outcomes reflect the intended behavior and not environment bugs, lucky runs, reward hacking, or unfair constraints.
items.quote: We then manually read through each of the 945 resulting transcripts. When agents succeed, we confirm that they succeeded for legitimate reasons, as opposed to getting lucky, or exploiting bugs in their environment or in the task’s scoring logic

items.claim: Has someone with no prior exposure attempt a scenario to surface ambiguities, unintended shortcuts and incidental difficulties before trusting it.
items.quote: For the majority of task families, we have an individual who has not been previously exposed to the family attempt a task in the family. They take notes on bugs they discover and ambiguities in the instructions or scoring logic.

items.claim: prefers human baselines under conditions identical to the agent's over informal time estimates or mismatched human-AI comparisons because only matched conditions ground the comparison.
items.quote: these typically don’t collect direct comparisons between human and AI performance, e.g. solely relying on informal time estimates (Jimenez et al., 2024), or comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (e.g. compute availability, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)

items.claim: Is candid that clean, unambiguous, auto-scorable, solitary tasks are an unrealistic feature of the benchmark and limit what its scores imply about real-world impact.
items.quote: The primary way in which HCAST tasks may be unrealistic is that each task has a limited and clearly defined scope. That is, the instructions for each task are designed to be unambiguous, with minimal additional context required to understand the task.

items.claim: Distrusts narrow evaluations that can be hill-climbed, so withholds most tasks and develops agents on a held-out dev set to avoid overfitting.
items.quote: We release 11 example task families from HCAST, but we withhold the rest to prevent data contamination, and to reduce hill-climbing against HCAST.

items.claim: Knowingly trades some realism for targeted capability measurement in a few tasks, and flags those tasks explicitly as less likely to appear in the real world.
items.quote: This task would be less likely to show up in the real world, but it still measures a targeted and informative set of skills.

items.claim: prefers treating agent results as a lower bound over claiming full capability because better prompting and scaffolding would likely raise performance.
items.quote: We believe our agent results are a reasonable lower bound, but better prompting and scaffolding is likely to improve performance. Future work will be necessary to determine the full capabilities of current frontier models.

items.claim: Focuses tasks on what models are actually used for and play to their strengths, expecting this to track real-world impact better than tasks they have not been optimized for.
items.quote: We expect this to track real-world impact more closely than tasks that AI systems have not been optimized to complete, given that in practice AI systems are differentially used to perform tasks where they’re advantaged.
